By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\).
Here \(f(x+h)-f(x)=\left[(x+h)^{2}+3(x+h)-1\right]-\left[x^{2}+3x-1\right]=2xh+h^{2}+3h\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{h(2x+h+3)}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}(2x+h+3)\)
\(\therefore f'(x)=2x+3\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin(3x+3h)-\sin 3x}{h}\).
Using \(\sin C-\sin D=2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\sin\frac{C-D}{2}\), the numerator is \(2\cos\left(3x+\frac{3h}{2}\right)\sin\frac{3h}{2}\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}3\cos\left(3x+\frac{3h}{2}\right)\cdot\frac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2}\)
As \(h \to 0\), \(\frac{\sin(3h/2)}{3h/2} \to 1\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=3\cos 3x\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{e^{2x+2h+1}-e^{2x+1}}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}e^{2x+1}\cdot\frac{e^{2h}-1}{h}\).
Writing \(\frac{e^{2h}-1}{h}=2\cdot\frac{e^{2h}-1}{2h}\) and using \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{e^{t}-1}{t}=1\),
\(\therefore f'(x)=2e^{2x+1}\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{3^{x+h}-3^{x}}{h}=3^{x}\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{3^{h}-1}{h}\).
Using the standard limit \(\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{a^{h}-1}{h}=\log a\) with \(a=3\),
\(\therefore f'(x)=3^{x}\log 3\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\log(2x+2h+5)-\log(2x+5)}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\log\left(1+\frac{2h}{2x+5}\right)\).
Put \(t=\frac{2h}{2x+5}\), so that \(\frac{1}{h}=\frac{2}{(2x+5)\,t}\) and \(t \to 0\) as \(h \to 0\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=\frac{2}{2x+5}\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\log(1+t)}{t}=\frac{2}{2x+5}\times 1\)
\(\therefore f'(x)=\frac{2}{2x+5}\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\tan(2x+2h+3)-\tan(2x+3)}{h}\).
Using \(\tan A-\tan B=\frac{\sin(A-B)}{\cos A\cos B}\) with \(A=2x+2h+3\), \(B=2x+3\), so \(A-B=2h\), the numerator becomes \(\frac{\sin 2h}{\cos(2x+2h+3)\cos(2x+3)}\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}2\cdot\frac{\sin 2h}{2h}\cdot\frac{1}{\cos(2x+2h+3)\cos(2x+3)}=\frac{2}{\cos^{2}(2x+3)}\)
\(\therefore f'(x)=2\sec^{2}(2x+3)\)

By the first principle, \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sec(5x+5h-2)-\sec(5x-2)}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\cos(5x-2)-\cos(5x+5h-2)}{h\,\cos(5x+5h-2)\cos(5x-2)}\).
Using \(\cos D-\cos C=2\sin\frac{C+D}{2}\sin\frac{C-D}{2}\), the numerator is \(2\sin\left(5x+\frac{5h}{2}-2\right)\sin\frac{5h}{2}\).
\(\therefore f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}5\sin\left(5x+\frac{5h}{2}-2\right)\cdot\frac{\sin(5h/2)}{5h/2}\cdot\frac{1}{\cos(5x+5h-2)\cos(5x-2)}=\frac{5\sin(5x-2)}{\cos^{2}(5x-2)}\)
\(\therefore f'(x)=5\sec(5x-2)\tan(5x-2)\)

Here \(f(x)=x\sqrt{x}=x^{3/2}\), so by the first principle \(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{3/2}-x^{3/2}}{h}\).
Multiplying and dividing by \((x+h)^{3/2}+x^{3/2}\),
\(f'(x)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{3}-x^{3}}{h\left[(x+h)^{3/2}+x^{3/2}\right]}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{h\left(3x^{2}+3xh+h^{2}\right)}{h\left[(x+h)^{3/2}+x^{3/2}\right]}=\frac{3x^{2}}{2x^{3/2}}\)
\(\therefore f'(x)=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2}\)

Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{2x+5}\), so \(f(2)=\sqrt{9}=3\).
By the first principle, \(f'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sqrt{2(2+h)+5}-3}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sqrt{9+2h}-3}{h}\).
Rationalising the numerator, \(f'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(9+2h)-9}{h\left(\sqrt{9+2h}+3\right)}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{2}{\sqrt{9+2h}+3}=\frac{2}{6}\)
\(\therefore f'(2)=\frac{1}{3}\)

Let \(f(x)=\tan x\), so \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1\).
By the first principle, \(f'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+h\right)-1}{h}\).
Since \(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+h\right)=\frac{1+\tan h}{1-\tan h}\), the numerator is \(\frac{1+\tan h}{1-\tan h}-1=\frac{2\tan h}{1-\tan h}\).
\(\therefore f'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0}2\cdot\frac{\tan h}{h}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\tan h}=2\times 1\times 1\)
\(\therefore f'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2\)

Let \(f(x)=\log(2x+1)\), so \(f(2)=\log 5\).
By the first principle, \(f'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\log(2(2+h)+1)-\log 5}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\log\left(\frac{5+2h}{5}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\log\left(1+\frac{2h}{5}\right)\).
\(=\frac{2}{5}\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\log\left(1+\frac{2h}{5}\right)}{\frac{2h}{5}}=\frac{2}{5}\times 1\), using \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\log(1+t)}{t}=1\).
\(\therefore f'(2)=\frac{2}{5}\)

Let \(f(x)=e^{3x-4}\), so \(f(2)=e^{2}\).
By the first principle, \(f'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{e^{3(2+h)-4}-e^{2}}{h}=e^{2}\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{e^{3h}-1}{h}=3e^{2}\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{e^{3h}-1}{3h}\).
Using \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{e^{t}-1}{t}=1\),
\(\therefore f'(2)=3e^{2}\)

Let \(f(x)=\cos x\). By the first principle, \(f'\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}+h\right)-\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}}{h}\).
Using \(\cos C-\cos D=-2\sin\frac{C+D}{2}\sin\frac{C-D}{2}\), the numerator is \(-2\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}+\frac{h}{2}\right)\sin\frac{h}{2}\).
\(\therefore f'\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=-\lim_{h \to 0}\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}+\frac{h}{2}\right)\cdot\frac{\sin(h/2)}{h/2}=-\sin\frac{5\pi}{4}=-\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\)
\(\therefore f'\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

Since \(x=-3\) falls in the branch \(x \ge -3\), \(f(-3)=2-3(-3)=11\).
Left-hand derivative: for \(h<0\) we have \(-3+h<-3\), so \(f(-3+h)=(-3+h)^{2}+2=11-6h+h^{2}\).
\(Lf'(-3)=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{\left(11-6h+h^{2}\right)-11}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}(-6+h)=-6\)
Right-hand derivative: for \(h>0\), \(f(-3+h)=2-3(-3+h)=11-3h\).
\(Rf'(-3)=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{(11-3h)-11}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}(-3)=-3\)
Since \(Lf'(-3)=-6 \ne -3=Rf'(-3)\), the two one-sided derivatives are unequal, so \(f'(-3)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) is not differentiable at \(x=-3\). (It is continuous there, since both one-sided limits equal \(11=f(-3)\) \(-\) continuity does not imply differentiability.)

Continuity: \(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=\lim_{x \to 0}x^{2}=0\) and \(f(0)=0^{2}=0\), so \(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=f(0)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x=0\).
Differentiability: \(f'(0)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{h^{2}-0}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}h=0\), which is finite, so the derivative exists.
\(\therefore f(x)=x^{2}\) is continuous and differentiable at \(x=0\), with \(f'(0)=0\).

Here \(f(0)=0\cdot|0|=0\).
Continuity: \(\left|f(x)\right|=\left|x\right|\cdot\left|x\right|=x^{2} \to 0\) as \(x \to 0\), so \(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=0=f(0)\), and \(f\) is continuous at \(x=0\).
Differentiability: \(Lf'(0)=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{h|h|-0}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}|h|=0\) and \(Rf'(0)=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{h|h|-0}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}|h|=0\).
The two one-sided derivatives agree, so \(f'(0)=0\) exists.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous and differentiable at \(x=0\).

At \(x=-\frac{3}{2}\) we have \(2x+3=0\), so \(f\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=0\).
Continuity: \(\left|f(x)\right|=\left|2x+3\right|\cdot\left|2x+3\right|=(2x+3)^{2} \to 0\) as \(x \to -\frac{3}{2}\), so \(\lim_{x \to -3/2}f(x)=0=f\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\) and \(f\) is continuous there.
Differentiability: for \(h \ne 0\), \(2\left(-\frac{3}{2}+h\right)+3=2h\), so \(f\left(-\frac{3}{2}+h\right)=2h\left|2h\right|=4h|h|\).
\(Lf'\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{4h|h|}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}4|h|=0\) and \(Rf'\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}4|h|=0\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous and differentiable at \(x=-\frac{3}{2}\), with \(f'\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=0\).

Here \(f(2)=[2]=2\).
For \(x\) just less than \(2\), i.e. \(1 \le x<2\), \([x]=1\), so \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}}f(x)=1\).
For \(x\) just greater than \(2\), i.e. \(2<x<3\), \([x]=2\), so \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}}f(x)=2\).
Since \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}}f(x)=1 \ne 2=\lim_{x \to 2^{+}}f(x)\), the limit does not exist and \(f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x=2\).
A function that is not continuous at a point cannot be differentiable there.
\(\therefore f\) is neither continuous nor differentiable at \(x=2\).

Since \(x=2\) falls in the branch \(x \le 2\), \(f(2)=12-2^{2}=8\).
Continuity: \(\lim_{x \to 2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x \to 2^{-}}\left(12-x^{2}\right)=8\) and \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x \to 2^{+}}(3x+2)=8\), both equal to \(f(2)=8\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x=2\).
Differentiability: \(Lf'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{\left[12-(2+h)^{2}\right]-8}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{-4h-h^{2}}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}(-4-h)=-4\)
\(Rf'(2)=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{\left[3(2+h)+2\right]-8}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{3h}{h}=3\)
Since \(-4 \ne 3\), \(f'(2)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(x=2\).

Since \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\) falls in the branch \(x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\sin\frac{\pi}{2}-\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=1-0=1\).
Continuity: \(\lim_{x \to \pi/2^{-}}(\sin x-\cos x)=1\) and \(\lim_{x \to \pi/2^{+}}(2x-\pi+1)=\pi-\pi+1=1\), both equal to \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Differentiability: \(Lf'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)\right]-1}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{\cos h+\sin h-1}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\left[\frac{\cos h-1}{h}+\frac{\sin h}{h}\right]=0+1=1\)
\(Rf'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{\left[2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)-\pi+1\right]-1}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{2h}{h}=2\)
Since \(1 \ne 2\), \(f'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) does not exist.
\(\therefore f\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

Continuity: for \(x \ne 0\), \(\left|\cos\frac{1}{x}\right| \le 1\), so \(0 \le \left|f(x)\right| \le x^{2}\). As \(x \to 0\), \(x^{2} \to 0\), hence by the squeeze theorem \(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=0=f(0)\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous at \(x=0\).
Differentiability: \(f'(0)=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{h^{2}\cos\frac{1}{h}-0}{h}=\lim_{h \to 0}h\cos\frac{1}{h}\).
Since \(0 \le \left|h\cos\frac{1}{h}\right| \le |h| \to 0\), this limit exists and equals \(0\).
\(\therefore f\) is continuous and differentiable at \(x=0\), with \(f'(0)=0\).
